paths.c4-1: Casts Partners’ patience as Nomad’s edge, notes zero investor turnover, and explains calling it a partnership rather than a fund.
paths.c4-2: Sets out the ‘equity yield curve’ against its bond-market namesake: time can lift equity returns while lowering their risk.
paths.c4-3: Disputes that long holding is futile, arguing greatness can be spotted ahead of time: the ‘longevity of compound’ opportunity.
paths.c4-4: Pictures a business’s future as branching paths whose odds improve along the way, which investors ignore, leaving long-run success unpriced.
paths.c4-5: Quotes Amazon on lengthening the time horizon: a seven-year view means competing against far fewer rivals than a three-year one.
paths.c14-1: Gell-Mann’s four stages of creative thought and Charles Jencks’s garden in Dumfries make the case for slow reflection between decisions.
paths.c14-2: With Taleb, reads the crisis as a shortage of slack: crammed diaries, maxed-out borrowing, cash never allowed to sit idle.
paths.c14-3: Klarman on Buffett: doing nothing is still a decision. Sleep and Zakaria expect their holdings to change little for years.
paths.c14-4: ‘Galactic HQ’ keeps studying a Glasgow office block, a Thai retailer and a drug maker, but deliberately trades nothing.
paths.c14-5: Treats inaction as value added, noting investee firms averaged about fifteen years old at purchase, so their runway is long.
paths.c5-1: Sizes positions with the Kelly criterion, via Bill Miller, and argues mass over-diversification is about marketing, not skill.
paths.c5-2: Challenges diversification as a safety rule, comparing it with slicing loans into securitisation trusts and trust-eroding outsourcing.
paths.c5-3: Treats diversification as industry dogma: many holdings reflect few insights, may add risk, and index funds do it cheaper.
paths.c11-1: Proposes admitting money only as new bargains appear, about one a month, which caps inflows near 5% of assets monthly.
paths.c11-2: Links reopening to the opportunity set, likely in a market panic, and thanks Partners who all subscribed within forty-eight hours.
paths.c11-3: Floats handing capital back to protect returns, unlike managers who follow Churchill’s keep-going advice, and asks Partners for their views.
paths.c11-4: Refuses to reopen merely for income, thanks to the cost-only fee; reports $1 grown to about $2.70, aiming for $10.
paths.c11-5: Proposes that any crisis fundraising use redeemable rights shares, so a Nomad swollen from $1bn to $4bn could shrink back.
paths.c1-1: Lists the three tests (half-price shares, owner-minded managers, sound capital allocation) and why a global remit helps find them.
paths.c1-2: Splits the portfolio into franchises, asset plays and workouts like Xerox; together priced at 51 cents per dollar of worth.
paths.c1-3: Two things drive results: paying about half of value, which patience controls, and managers’ capital allocation, which takes judgement.
paths.c1-4: Half-price purchases plus 10% yearly value growth imply about 26% a year; Readers Digest illustrates the common capital-allocation mistake.
paths.c1-5: Reprints the 2005 plea to watch price-to-value, not price, using brain research on why stress makes immediate gains feel bigger.
paths.c10-1: Hunting for corporate character: the questions put to managers, Lynch’s diworsification, and a first stock screen in twelve years.
paths.c10-2: Introduces the fifteen-strong ‘super-high-quality thinkers’ list, the ‘terminal portfolio’, citing Stagecoach’s shrinking and National Indemnity’s pricing discipline.
paths.c10-3: In Asia, Sleep sides with dynastic family owners, who act as principals, against foreign agents and a gambling crowd.
paths.c10-4: Henry Royce making engineers sign their parts is set against modern efficiency and securitisation, which build no lasting reputation.
paths.c10-5: Estimates under five percent of listed firms act on conviction rather than for applause; most Nomad holdings are among them.
paths.c16-1: Compares behavioural finance to geography: a mix of economics, psychology and biology, because humans make the decisions.
paths.c16-2: Sleep and Zakaria’s reasons for joining the Santa Fe Institute, founded by Gell-Mann and Los Alamos scientists to bridge disciplines.
paths.c16-3: Uses Rangaswami’s food analogy for information: foragers versus fenced farms like patent law, and a served steak versus raw data.
paths.c9-1: Union Cement, priced near a quarter of replacement cost: Holcim paid five times Nomad’s average, but shares barely traded.
paths.c9-2: Zimcem, Siam Cement and Pretoria Portland Cement illustrate the model: assets need replacing, so prices must rise to fund it.
paths.c9-3: Recalls mid-2000s Zimbabwe, where near-monopoly cement plants and breweries sold for a small fraction of what they cost to build.
paths.c6-1: Sleep and Zakaria aim to act as principals rather than milk the conflict, and float someday waiving the performance fee.
paths.c6-2: Leaving Marathon, Sleep and Zakaria put fair fees first, rejecting hedge-fund norms for a deal that feels even decades on.
paths.c6-3: Recasts the conflict as long-term founders against quarter-by-quarter traders who set prices, the gap Nomad’s ten main stocks rely on.
paths.c6-4: Laments the loss of trust, once so central that it named unit trusts and trustees, under heavy-handed governance rules.
paths.c6-5: Nomad’s cost-only fee falls from about 50 to near 10 basis points, saving mostly charitable Partners roughly $15m a year.
paths.c7-1: An appendix quotation on consistency and commitment bias: how hard-won, publicly stated conclusions become the hardest to abandon.
paths.c7-2: Illustrates availability bias with Dick Thaler’s ball-passing video, in which almost nobody notices a person in a gorilla suit.
paths.c7-3: The poisonous-plant analogy: brains learn from quick feedback, so long-term investors, lacking it, easily misread cause and effect.
paths.c7-4: Richard Zeckhauser’s Norway-area quiz at Harvard, with percentile ranges, shows how overconfident people are about things they don’t know.
paths.c7-5: A panellist dismisses Zimbabwe on sight; Munger’s egg quip and car adverts read after purchase show bad associations blocking thought.
paths.c12-1: Criticises mandates boxing managers by region, sector, style or size, then introduces a staff notice from Erie Indemnity’s founder.
paths.c12-2: Concedes hedge funds have a point on bureaucracy, admits Nomad drifts too, and ties Munger’s deserved trust to thinking.
paths.c12-3: Locates the real risk in constrained funds not in the mandate but in the unthinking managers who run them.
paths.c12-4: Regulation, accounting rules and due diligence drain honest managers, who cannot escape overbearing oversight however well they behave.
paths.c12-5: Regulated like a leveraged hedge fund, Nomad must disprove being Madoff; Sleep prefers sleuthing regulators and taxing short-term investing.
paths.c8-1: Drops two pet beliefs: Conseco showed a low share price can hurt, Northwest Airlines that heavy insider ownership can too.
paths.c8-2: Selling Apple cost Nomad more than holding Northwest Airlines, yet clients ask only about Northwest: opportunity costs stay invisible.
paths.c8-3: Keeps Amazon after it doubles, since selling an early Wal-Mart is the costliest error; selling Stagecoach hurt more than Conseco.
paths.c8-4: Sleep swaps the plural for the first person to own his many mistakes, neither excusing nor condemning them, only learning.
paths.c8-5: Promises to walk through three recent wrong-looking purchases on three continents, joking that Nomad’s buying is a kiss of death.
paths.c13-1: Sets a rough 10% ownership threshold for influencing outcomes and warns that liquidity-minded investors with tiny stakes have no voice.
paths.c13-2: Large outside shareholders acting as general partners: Brandes at Jardine Matheson, Allan Gray at Kersaf, Tweedy Browne at Hollinger.
paths.c13-3: Restates the case for owning over 10%, specifying the UK, and argues tiny, liquid holdings leave investors powerless over outcomes.
paths.c13-4: Big holders backstopping rights issues can remove dilution risk, as Wilbur Ross’s $750m pledge to Assured Guaranty shows, unlike MBIA.
paths.c13-5: Gives the recipe (spot lasting success, buy early, own enough to matter) and asks why prices miss it.
paths.c2-1: Costco exemplifies ‘scale efficiencies shared’, growing by giving back; few firms asked about windfalls would hand them to customers.
paths.c2-2: Bezos on why Amazon keeps cutting prices despite short-term elasticity maths, trusting judgement that it builds long-run cash flow.
paths.c2-3: Defines the loop of lower prices and customer reciprocation; Costco sells four times more per foot than ordinary supermarkets.
paths.c2-4: Lists practitioners from Ryanair to Tesco and notes such firms, Costco to AirAsia, form about sixty percent of Nomad.
paths.c2-5: Low costs and thin margins form a virtuous spiral that outweighs daily noise; leads into Bezos’s Wired interview.
paths.c3-1: Early Buffett Partnership letters explain why the order of yearly returns doesn’t matter: analysis decides whether, markets decide when.
paths.c3-2: Prefers compounded multi-year results to annual figures, because Nomad controls whether it is right but not when.
paths.c3-3: Taleb’s paper: investors accept rare big losses for steady small wins, preferring a comfortable ride to a better destination.
paths.c3-4: Trailing the index this year, Sleep calls it merely one opportunity set and targets returns like Ruane’s, Klarman’s or Schloss’s.
paths.c3-5: Suggests pooling good years with bad and dropping the adjectives: whatever the order of returns, the destination stays the same.
paths.c15-1: Dismisses the growth-versus-value debate using Buffett: low price-to-book or high yield neither proves nor rules out value.

voice.humour-1: Deadpan advice for dying rich: swap stocks for bonds in each boom, then back again in each panic.
voice.humour-2: Mocks acronym-laden exotica as investment Viagras: should Nomad ever seek them, everyone, founders included, should sell.
voice.humour-3: A Harare paper still printing rates for defunct European currencies, and a headline about grabbing wireless phone lines.
voice.humour-4: Zakaria’s joke: asked how he is at a party, a hedge fund manager replies with his monthly return.
voice.humour-5: Blenkinsopp’s excuses to his teacher, four dead grandmothers and all, introduce the handover update.
voice.humour-6: Encloses Terry Arthur’s book 95% is Crap, bought cheaply on Amazon, where Partners should buy gift copies too.
voice.humour-7: Sleep overpays for a chrome S at the Savoy auction, showing scarcity and social proof at work.
voice.humour-8: Braced for £15,000, a buyer is billed £1,500 for two Bond cars, then swaps one for a GTO.
voice.humour-9: Jokes about a Nomad Inactivity App, sold only through Amazon, for live updates on the absence of trading.
voice.humour-10: After a grim Zimbabwe saga, each Partner gets a worthless hundred-trillion-dollar Zimbabwean note as a souvenir to frame.
voice.candour-1: Admits missing Monsanto’s indemnity for Solutia’s environmental liabilities, found later in SEC filings, and selling near cost.
voice.candour-2: Sleep concedes he misjudged Argentina three years earlier by over-weighting vivid, temporary evidence, at real cost.
voice.candour-3: Names selling Stagecoach, which kept climbing, as a bigger error than buying Conseco, since missed gains go unrecorded.
voice.candour-4: Conseco: anchoring on the original case to keep holding cost about $5m, or roughly $10m counting opportunity cost.
voice.candour-5: Owns up to misreading dilution risk at MBIA, costing Partners roughly 1.5% of net assets this year.
voice.candour-6: Sleep and Zakaria admit falling for firms’ revenue and margin promises without checking how they would be earned.
voice.critique-1: Attacks insider buyouts like Weetabix via Schemes of Arrangement, and fund managers who sell cheaply without complaint.
voice.critique-2: Faults the industry’s price-to-book style shortcuts, which survive through lazy thinking and marketing spin, not investment merit.
voice.critique-3: Blames wealthy institutions for indulging pointless reporting demands and for trading daily in what is permanent capital.
voice.critique-4: Criticises copycat hedge-fund fee scales and a bank earning 25% on equity that cannot handle Nomad’s refundable fee.
voice.critique-5: Attacks seeing the index as riskless, which breeds over-diversification; index-hugging funds sell because clients distrust their managers.
voice.critique-6: Targets diversification dogma and salami-sliced securitised loans, which dress up ignorance as an asset and erode customer trust.
